title.narrative: Fiscal Governance and Financial Sector Reforms Program (Subprogram 1)

description.narrative:
1.The proposed effort to design and process a Kazakhstan Fiscal Governance and Financial Sector Reforms Program (the Program) aims to help the Government of Kazakhstan (government) address one of its core development challenges: heightened macroeconomic and financial vulnerability to external shocks. This medium-term development objective requires specific reform and institutional developments in fiscal management and in financial sector development. Under preparation since mid-2021 with an initially wider list of reform pillars (five) and proposals and the agreement to subsequently prioritize the subset of reform items with more agreement and progress, this approach was disrupted by the January 2022 political crisis in Kazakhstan and the political transition that ensued. The geopolitical and new economic realities set in motion by the Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 also added further disruptions in the country's economic policy agenda during early-2022. At the request of Government, active discussions on the program resumed in May 2022, and momentum was regained with the new approval by the President of reform strategic directions along the then-already agreed two reform pillars of the program (and to which past preparatory dialogue had contributed).
2.The scope of the proposed two-subprogram programmatic assistance is fully consistent with the government's strategic priorities, with the forthcoming Asian Development Bank (ADB) country partnership strategy for Kazakhstan, and with the ADB Strategy 2030, namely three of its operational priorities. The proposed programmatic approach provides inherent and much-needed flexibility in medium-term reform directions while recognizing current achievements and formalizing medium-term reform commitments that are a primer for Kazakhstan.

1.1. To enable proper sequencing in the Public Financial Management and Fiscal reforms agenda, and ensure long-term fiscal sustainability and cyclical macro-fiscal policy consistency: (i) The Government approved the Public Financial Management Concept Decree (by order of the President), setting, inter alia, explicit fiscal consolidation (and quantitative) targets (till 2030) for non-oil deficit, overall deficit, public debt (as a ceiling), government debt (as a ceiling), NFRK assets, net financial assets ratio (NFRK/financial debt ratio), government debt service as a percentage of budget expenditures (as a ceiling); (ii) New Fiscal Rules were approved to govern fiscal policy (non-oil deficit path) in a way that becomes countercyclical and imposes annual limits for transfers from NFRK (through Parliament ratification of amendments to the Budget Code); (iii) New debt service limits for municipalities (through MNE decree); (iv) The Government approved (via decree) the expanded scope of formal monitoring of external and domestic debt of all state-owned enterprises.

1.2. To eliminate pressing and problematic fiscal distortions related to PPP procurement, and to start addressing constraints to the viability of public investments: (i) The MNE established (a) limits to state obligations in PPPs and other concessions for each region, (b) new rules for selection of concession projects and for conducting tenders and tender preparation work (eliminating exclusive rights for advisory services and introducing open competition), (c) a prohibition to SOEs participating in PPPs as private partner, (d) mandatory competitive processes for USPs and a strict restriction on direct selection. (ii) The Government (a) established and operationalized a dedicated module on public investments under the SPIS, (b) developed and approved a new and binding methodology for PIM that governs the economic appraisal and prioritization of public investment proposals at pre-feasibility stage, the feasibility stage, and the financing and decision-making on procurement after the feasibility stage, (c) approved PPP fiscal affordability limits for an expanded list of government support measures for mandatory compliance by all government bodies.

1.3. To enhance fiscal transparency, address key risks to fiscal sustainability (including from climate change and climate change action)—and to reduce costly biases towards off-budget solutions—through the establishment of fiscal risk management functions and public disclosure of fiscal risks, the: (i) Parliament amended the Budget Code to impose the obligation for government to disclose, with the annual budget submission to Parliament, a fiscal sustainability and risks assessment; (ii) Government disclosed the first ever fiscal sustainability and risks assessments to Parliament, including a budget risks assessment component, a specific fiscal risks component, and a long-term fiscal sustainability assessments component that also recognizes the fiscal implications of a ‘decarbonization scenario' in Kazakhstan; (iii) Government submitted a joint decree to Parliament (as an attachment to the new Budget Code), that sets the process, distribution of analytical work, and structure of the annual fiscal risks statement that is required in each state budget submission to Parliament.

1.4. To enable credibility and transparency in public finances, the Government started the transition to accrual budgeting at subnational levels through the following MOF instructions/decisions: (i) Issuance of ‘Rules for Preparation of Forecast Consolidated Financial Statements' for regional budgets, and budget of the cities of republican significance and the capital city; (ii) Mandatory instructions to all regions, cities of republican significance, and the capital city for the preparation of 2023 budget submissions in accordance with the new rules.

1.5. To mainstream gender equality in public financial management, the Government: (i) updated the Family and Gender Policy 2030, approving the corresponding Action Plan, which includes specific actions to: (a) introduce gender-responsive budgeting (GRB); (b) implement GRB pilots based on gender needs assessment; (ii) conducted pilot gender-sensitive review of public expenditures in social sectors and submits with recommendations to United Nations as integral section of 2022 Voluntary National Review; and (iii) introduced (via order of the Bureau of National Statistics) requirements for gender-disaggregated data in statistics collection.

1.6. To strengthen and institutionalize government support for women entrepreneurship the Government approved a dedicated budget financing of T800 million for Women Entrepreneurship Development Centers (WEDCs), established in all regions of Kazakhstan and offering training and business development services, in 2023 State Budget.

1.7. To ensure strategic consistency (including in market communication) and medium-term debt sustainability, and establish active and forward-looking liability management practices that are also conducive to the development of a government securities market: (i) The Parliament approved amendments to Law on Budget Systems to give MOF the legal authority to implement active liability management (ALM) operations and any debt issuance strategy deemed necessary; (ii) The Government approved amendments to Government Decree to establish comprehensive debt analysis of all direct and contingent liabilities (by MNE and MOF), including SOE debt and PPP liabilities; (iii) The Government established a debt management policy to govern medium-term debt management strategy, and to initiate its market communication, the MOF formulated and conducted stakeholder consultations on the first Medium-Term Debt Strategy for 2023-2025 and corresponding action plan, with explicit objectives with regards to cost-risk minimization and development of the government securities market; (iv) The Government approved an ALM framework, through (a) new policy and governance rules on ALM and communications to cover bond buy-backs and switches, (b) a time-bound debt benchmark development and debt consolidation roadmap and quantitative targets for 2023-3025, and (c) public disclosure of debt issuance plans and schedules, ensuring compliance with such schedules. (v) The Parliament approved a new legal framework on “netting arrangements” (new legal framework on close-out netting, or netting law) in Kazakhstan, amending several other existing laws to e.g., reduce risks in repo transactions, as an effort to develop liquid secured interbank markets and strengthen the role of government securities as the collateral of choice in money markets.

1.8. To gradually enable an effective introduction of climate policy accounting and assessment concepts and instruments, such as ESG, EIA and green budget tagging, the Government approved and implemented: (i) Energy efficiency improvement plans for social sectors and urban services under Green Kazakhstan National Project; (ii) Full SDG-alignment of budget expenditure classification and climate-related SDG tagging of actual budget expenditures for 2019-2021, as part of the Rapid Integrated Assessment of selected budget programs (which was submitted to the UN within the Second Voluntary National Report [2022]).

2.1. To set ESG-sensitive strategic objectives and high-level instructions for financial sector reform and the development of the financial sector (to, amongst other objectives, enhance governance and financial stability, and to resolve long-standing structural weaknesses in the sector) in a way that is properly sequenced and effectively coordinated: (i) the Strategic Concept for ‘Development of the Financial Sector of Kazakhstan until 2030' was approved by Presidential Decree, together with a time-bound implementation action-plan for implementing agencies' compliance; (ii) the government initiated the implementation of the action-plan and conducted (through the ARDFM) regular monitoring of its implementation (with duly published reports, quarterly); (iii) Parliament approved amendments to legal framework on AML/FCT to introduce an operational definition of Politically Exposed Person (PEP); (iv) The ARDFM (a) integrated an AML/CFT risk assessment component into its risk-based supervision system, (b) approved a methodology for internal procedures on ICAAP and ILAAP, and (c) approved the regulatory changes to introduce PEP screening in its review and approval process for large equity investment proposals into commercial banks; (v) The Agency for Financial Monitoring strengthened consumer protection by approving and implementing methodologies for identification of financial pyramids and Ponzi schemes.

2.2. To enhance the confidence in, and the effectiveness of the deposit insurance safety net, legislative amendments and operational modifications were implemented to: (i) ensure risk-based pricing of premiums by second-tier banks into the reserve fund; and (ii) ensure payouts within 1 year after bank license revocation (including transfer to pension accounts in last resort).

2.3. To enhance the effectiveness of the regulatory framework and of banking supervision practices, the AFDRM: (i) introduced annual Asset Quality Review (AQR) into its supervisory practice implementation; (ii) expanded the scope of this new supervisory practice by completing the AQR at the consolidated system level (>70% of the system aggregated assets), and duly publishing the AQR report; (iii) in support of full transition to Basel III, (a) started applying the supervisory process according to the SREP methodology, annually, (b) determined recommendations based on the results of the SREP and started monitoring bank's implementation, (c) started publishing the results of the SREP, annually, in the “Priorities of Supervision”.

2.4. To improve transparency with regards to non-performing loans (NPLs), create conditions for the development of an active market for Non-Performing Assets (as a mechanism to eliminate bad asset legacies from past macro shocks, and enable faster recoveries by the financial system in the future), and to establish reliable and socially-responsible personal bankruptcy and solvency restoration options that do not disrupt creditors' rights: (i) The ARDFM conducted an annual comprehensive assessment of the quality of NPLs (calibration and classification) that included assessment of selected off-balance sheet items related to NPLs using IFRS 9 (i.e., including Stage 2 and Stage 3 loans); (ii) The Parliament approved a new law and considered amendments to the tax code to (a) eliminate legal obstacles to allow a wide range of private investors, including international investors interested in acquiring NPLs from banks, non-banks and microfinance institutions, to enter the market, (b) provide a favorable tax treatment to non-recourse buyers of distressed assets (e.g. tax treatment on corporate income tax [cash-method]), (c) introduce the institute of service companies which will provide services to investors on maintenance and management of non-performing assets, (d) set time limits of 3 years for holding the recovered property on the balance-sheet of banks, non-banking, and microfinance organizations. (iii) The Parliament approved a new law to create three options for personal bankruptcy at the initiative/discretion of the debtor (out-of-court, free of charge; judicial, to be run by financial administrator; procedure for restoration of solvency, to be run by financial manager).

2.5. To promote sustainable banking practices and eliminate regulatory risk, the ARDFM issued regulatory guidance (through Agency Chairperson orders) on the disclosure of information about the degree of exposure to ESG-related risks, as well as the procedure for identifying, assessing, and managing such risks in accordance with international ESG disclosure standards.

2.6. To credibly mainstream ESG considerations across the financial sector and promote green finance, the: (i) The Government established eligibility criteria for green projects for financing through green bonds and loans by approving the Decree on Green Taxonomy, thereby enabling mobilization of resources for and targeting of ESG-responsive investments; (ii) The KASE established and operationalized the regulated framework and approved the list of organizations that can provide ESG-compliance accreditation to all listed ESG-compliant securities, in order to establish credibility in the ESG bonds as a new asset class; (iii) The KASE established and operationalized a regulated framework of relief for the payment of listing fees for ESG bond issuers as well as targeted consulting support, thereby promoting ESG business as the driver of this new asset class; (iv) Parliament approved legal amendments to enable borrowing by local municipalities (of cities of republican significance) from international financial institutions to finance “green” projects.

Action 6: 1.14. To credibly mainstream ESG considerations across the financial sector and promote green finance, the: (i) The Government established eligibility criteria for green projects for financing through green bonds and loans by approving the Decree on Green Taxonomy, thereby enabling mobilization of resources for and targeting of ESG-responsive investments; (ii) The KASE established and operationalized the regulated framework and approved the list of organizations that can provide ESG-compliance accreditation to all listed ESG-compliant securities, in order to establish credibility in the ESG bonds as a new asset class; (iii) The KASE established and operationalized a regulated framework of relief for the payment of listing fees for ESG bond issuers as well as targeted consulting support, thereby promoting ESG business as the driver of this new asset class; (iv) Parliament approved legal amendments to enable borrowing by local municipalities (of cities of republican significance) from international financial institutions to finance “green” projects. Target date: 2023-10-31
